reference.source: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours
clinicalPearls: The commonest malignant sex cord-stromal tumour, typically oestrogen-secreting and behaving as a low-grade malignancy with a tendency to late recurrence
The adult type usually presents in peri- and postmenopausal women, while the rarer juvenile type occurs in girls and young women
Oestrogen excess causes postmenopausal bleeding, endometrial hyperplasia, or even endometrial carcinoma in adults, and precocious pseudopuberty in children
Serum inhibin and anti-Mullerian hormone are useful tumour markers that reflect disease burden and help detect recurrence
Histology characteristically shows Call-Exner bodies (rosette-like arrangements around eosinophilic material) and grooved coffee-bean nuclei in the adult type
Adult granulosa cell tumours are strongly associated with a recurrent FOXL2 gene mutation
Because relapse can occur many years after treatment, prolonged follow-up is essential
Large tumours may present acutely with haemoperitoneum from rupture
reference.pathophysiology: Granulosa cell tumours are sex cord-stromal neoplasms derived from the granulosa cells of the ovarian follicle, often accompanied by a thecal component. They commonly retain the hormonal function of their cell of origin and secrete oestrogen, and sometimes inhibin, which underlies both the clinical syndrome and the useful tumour markers. In the adult type, a characteristic somatic FOXL2 mutation is central to tumorigenesis, and the cells arrange themselves into microfollicular, trabecular, or diffuse patterns, sometimes forming Call-Exner bodies. Unopposed oestrogen stimulation of the endometrium explains the associated hyperplasia and increased risk of endometrial carcinoma. These tumours are indolent but genuinely malignant, with a propensity for local recurrence and spread within the abdomen, sometimes decades after the initial diagnosis.
additionalDifferentials: Other sex cord-stromal tumours such as Sertoli-Leydig cell tumour
Small cell carcinoma of the ovary
Metastatic carcinoma with a luteinised stroma
additionalInvestigations: Transvaginal ultrasound to characterise a solid or mixed ovarian mass
Serum inhibin and anti-Mullerian hormone as tumour markers, with oestradiol where relevant
Endometrial assessment (biopsy or hysteroscopy) to detect hyperplasia or carcinoma from oestrogen excess
Cross-sectional imaging for staging and detection of recurrence
CA125 to help distinguish from epithelial ovarian cancer
Histology with immunohistochemistry (e.g. inhibin, calretinin, FOXL2) to confirm the diagnosis
redFlags: Postmenopausal bleeding with an ovarian mass, mandating endometrial evaluation for hyperplasia or carcinoma
Acute abdominal pain and signs of haemoperitoneum from tumour rupture
Precocious puberty in a girl with a pelvic mass
Recurrent disease presenting years after apparently successful treatment
reference.prognosis: Most adult granulosa cell tumours are diagnosed at an early stage and have a favourable long-term outlook, but their tendency to recur late means survival curves continue to fall over decades; advanced stage and rupture worsen the prognosis. Juvenile tumours are usually cured when confined to the ovary.
pitfalls: Failing to evaluate the endometrium for hyperplasia or carcinoma driven by oestrogen excess
Discharging patients from follow-up too early given the risk of very late recurrence
Misclassifying the tumour as an epithelial ovarian cancer and mismanaging it
Overlooking rupture as a cause of acute presentation and adverse staging
references: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours
Blaustein's Pathology of the Female Genital Tract
management: Surgery is the mainstay, with surgical staging and salpingo-oophorectomy, and fertility-sparing unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy reasonable in young women with disease confined to one ovary
Assess and treat the endometrium for oestrogen-driven hyperplasia or coexisting carcinoma with biopsy or hysteroscopy
Consider platinum-based adjuvant chemotherapy for advanced-stage or high-risk disease
Undertake prolonged surveillance with serum inhibin and anti-Mullerian hormone given the tendency to late recurrence
Manage recurrence with cytoreductive surgery, further chemotherapy or hormonal therapy such as aromatase inhibitors
Manage within a gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary team, confirming diagnosis with inhibin, calretinin and FOXL2 immunohistochemistry
